"'''Nosedive'''" is the first episode in the third series of the British [[Science fiction on television|science fiction]] [[anthology series]] ''[[Black Mirror]]''. [[Michael Schur]] and [[Rashida Jones]] wrote the [[teleplay]] for the episode, based on a story by series creator and co-showrunner [[Charlie Brooker]], while [[Joe Wright]] acted as director. It premiered on [[Netflix]] on 21 October 2016, alongside the rest of the third series. The episode is set in a world where people can rate each other from one to five stars, using their [[smartphone]]s, for every interaction they have, which can impact their [[socioeconomic status]]. Lacie ([[Bryce Dallas Howard]]) is a young woman overly obsessed with her ratings; she finds an opportunity to elevate her ratings greatly and move into a more luxurious residence after being chosen by her popular childhood, highly rated friend ([[Alice Eve]]) as the maid of honour for her wedding.

Under Netflix, the episode was given a much larger budget than the previous episodes of the programme, when it had been under [[Channel 4]]. Brooker wrote an outline for the episode, then Schur wrote the first half of the episode and Jones wrote the latter. Production was undertaken in a manner similar to a short film; "Nosedive" was filmed in [[South Africa]], with [[Seamus McGarvey]] as [[director of photography]] and Joel Collins and James Foster as the [[production designers]]. The tone of the episode is less bleak and more comedic than other ''Black Mirror'' episodes, with the ending significantly more positive than in episodes of the programme's prior two series.

The episode received mainly positive reviews and is middling in critics' lists of ''Black Mirror'' episodes, qualitatively. The pastel visual aesthetics were widely praised, along with [[Max Richter]]'s soundtrack and Howard's performance. A criticism from several reviewers was the episode's predictability and ending, though the script and comedic undertones were praised by some. Many critics noted the similarity of the episode to real-world app [[Peeple (mobile application)|Peeple]] and China's [[Social Credit System]], along with fictional works about social media with themes of gender and obsession with image. The episode won a [[Royal Television Society Craft & Design Award]]. It was nominated for several awards, including a [[Screen Actors Guild Award]] nomination for Howard and a [[Primetime Emmy Award]] nomination for McGarvey. A board game ''Nosedive'', based on the episode, was released in 2018.

==Plot==
Society has embraced a technology wherein everyone shares their daily activities and user experiences through [[eye implant]]s and mobile devices where one rates their interactions with others on a scale from one to five stars, cumulatively affecting everyone's [[socioeconomic status]].

Lacie Pound ([[Bryce Dallas Howard]]) seeks to raise her 4.2 rating to 4.5 for a discount on a luxury apartment at Pelican Cove, as her current lease is expiring and the agent warns that units are in high demand; however, despite her attempts to be outgoing and pleasant, her rating has stagnated. Lacie talks to a consultant who suggests gaining favour from very highly rated people. Lacie uploads a photograph of Mr. Rags, a [[Rag doll|ragdoll]] that she and her childhood friend Naomi ([[Alice Eve]]) made together. Naomi, who is currently rated 4.8, rates the photo five stars and calls Lacie to announce her engagement, inviting Lacie to deliver a wedding speech as the [[maid of honour]]. Learning that the wedding will be attended by hundreds of guests whom all have a rating of 4.7 or above, Lacie accepts the invitation and impulsively commits to the apartment, anticipating that their high ratings will easily secure her the necessary 4.5 score.

On the day of her flight, several mishaps cause people to rate Lacie negatively. This drops her rating down to 4.183. At the airport, her flight is cancelled and she cannot book a seat on an alternate flight without being a 4.2 or above. This agitates Lacie and she causes a scene, upon which security penalizes her by putting her on "double damage" and subtracting a full point for 24 hours. Because of her low rating, Lacie can only rent an older car to drive to the wedding, which she cannot recharge when it runs out of power. She is forced to [[Hitchhiking|hitchhike]] with Susan ([[Cherry Jones]]), a truck driver with a rating of 1.4. Susan reveals she used to be a 4.6, and tells Lacie that she used to care about her rating until her late husband was passed over for vital [[cancer treatment]] because his score was deemed not high enough. Susan says she is much freer without obsessing over ratings.

While Lacie is on the route to the wedding, Naomi tells her to not come, as her severely reduced rating will negatively impact Naomi's own ratings. Enraged, Lacie reaches the wedding and sneaks in during the reception. She grabs the microphone and starts giving the speech she had written but insults Naomi with references to childhood conflict, such as sleeping with Lacie's high school boyfriend. Security attempts to apprehend her, upon which Lacie grabs a knife and threatens to behead Mr. Rags. Still on double damage, the guests downvote her in droves, causing her rating to drop below one star. Lacie is imprisoned with her eye implants removed, but is genuinely happy for the first time in a long time. She and the man in the cell opposite hers ([[Sope Dirisu]]), realizing they can now speak without worrying about being rated, gleefully hurl insults at each other.

"Nosedive" is the first episode of the third series of ''Black Mirror''; all six episodes in this series were released on Netflix simultaneously on 21 October 2016. Brooker says it was selected to be the season premiere "partly to slightly ease people in",<ref name="worst year ever">{{cite web|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/tv/features/black-mirror-season-3-charlie-brooker-interview-release-date-joe-wright-nosedive-shut-up-and-dance-a7372841.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220621/https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/tv/features/black-mirror-season-3-charlie-brooker-interview-release-date-joe-wright-nosedive-shut-up-and-dance-a7372841.html |archive-date=21 June 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|title=Black Mirror co-creator Charlie Brooker: 'I'm loath to say this is the worst year ever because the next is coming'|date=21 October 2016|work=[[The Independent]]|last=Stolworthy|first=Jacob|access-date=31 August 2017}}</ref> at Netflix's recommendation.<ref name="ibm"/> Alongside "[[San Junipero]]", "Nosedive" was first shown in 2016 ahead of its Netflix release at the [[2016 Toronto International Film Festival|Toronto International Film Festival]].<ref name="collider"/> Two days prior to the series' release on Netflix, Brooker hinted that "Nosedive" is "a pastel, playful satire about modern insecurity."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/black-mirror-series-3-interview-charlie-brooker-and-annabel-jones/|title=Black Mirror series 3 interview: Charlie Brooker and Annabel Jones|work=Den of Geek!|publisher=[[Dennis Publishing]]|last=Mellor|first=Louisa|date=19 October 2016|access-date=31 August 2017}}</ref>

Whilst series one and two of ''Black Mirror'' were shown on [[Channel 4]] in the UK, in September 2015 Netflix commissioned the series for 12 episodes (split into two series of six episodes),<ref>{{cite web|url=https://variety.com/2015/digital/news/netflix-black-mirror-new-episodes-1201602037/|title=Netflix Picks Up 'Black Mirror' for 12 New Episodes|first=Debra |last=Birnbaum|work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=25 September 2016|access-date=26 December 2017}}</ref> and in March 2016 it outbid Channel 4 for the rights to distributing the third series, with a bid of $40 million.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2016/mar/29/netflix-channel-4-charlie-brooker-black-mirror |title=Netflix deals Channel 4 knockout blow over Charlie Brooker's Black Mirror |first=John |last=Plunkett |date=29 March 2016 |newspaper=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref> Due to its move to Netflix, the show had a larger budget than in previous series,<ref name="Guardian Lee"/> which one critic suggests is responsible for the "impressive line-up" that was noted by many reviewers.<ref name="telegraph"/> Another critic called this episode the show's "most ambitious yet";<ref name="Independent Community">{{cite web|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/tv/news/black-mirror-season-3-episode-nosedive-community-meow-meow-beanz-a7376651.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220621/https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/tv/news/black-mirror-season-3-episode-nosedive-community-meow-meow-beanz-a7376651.html |archive-date=21 June 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|title=Black Mirror season 3 episode 'Nosedive' is very similar to Community episode 'App Development and Condiments'|last=Shepherd|first=Jack|work=[[The Independent]]|date=23 October 2016|access-date=12 August 2017}}</ref> due to its larger episode order, series 3 was also able to vary its genre and tone more than previous series.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/10/21/arts/television/review-black-mirror-finds-terror-and-soul-in-the-machine.html|title=Review: 'Black Mirror' Finds Terror, and Soul, in the Machine|work=[[The New York Times]]|last=Poniewozik|first=James|date=20 October 2016|access-date=12 August 2017}}</ref> One reviewer also noted that "Nosedive" contained "only American characters".<ref name="collider"/>

In November 2016, to tie in with the episode, Netflix released a tongue-in-cheek app called Rate Me. The app allows users to rate people, by their [[Twitter]] handle, and view their own rating and the ratings of others.<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://www.wired.co.uk/article/rate-me-nosedive-black-mirror-netflix|title=Black Mirror's horrific people-rating app is now a reality. Sort of|magazine=[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]]|publisher=[[Condé Nast]]|last=Temperton|first=James|date=10 November 2016|access-date=1 September 2017}}</ref>

===Conception and writing===
{{multiple image
| align       = right
| image1      = Rashida Jones at 2017 MIFF (cropped).jpg
| total_width = 350
| alt1        = A 42 year-old woman looking at the camera.
| image2      = Michael Schur 2012 (cropped).jpg
| alt2        = An approximately 35 year-old man looking at the camera.
| footer      = [[Rashida Jones]] ''(left)'' and [[Michael Schur]] ''(right)'' co-wrote the script.}}

The episode is based on an idea by series creator [[Charlie Brooker]] for a movie; he and executive producer [[Annabel Jones]] pitched the idea to several movie companies in the United States after the first series of ''Black Mirror'', but it was not commissioned.<ref name="ibm">{{cite book | title=Inside Black Mirror | date=November 2018 | first1=Charlie | last1=Brooker | first2=Annabel | last2=Jones | first3=Jason | last3=Arnopp | chapter=Nosedive | isbn=9781984823489 | publisher=[[Crown Publishing Group]] | place=New York City}}</ref> The original idea was of a comedy similar to ''[[Brewster's Millions]]'', focused on a high status person trying to reduce their ranking in 24 hours.<ref name="ibm"/><ref name="Decider"/> Later, Brooker wrote either a three<ref name="ew interview"/> or four<ref name="avclub interview"/> page outline for the episode, wanting it to be "comedic, darkly".<ref name="ew interview"/> This version took inspiration from 1987 film ''[[Planes, Trains and Automobiles]]'', in which the character is on a journey—for "Nosedive", this was initially a character travelling to an important work presentation.<ref name="ibm"/>

[[Rashida Jones]] and [[Michael Schur]] wrote the episode. Known for comedy and sitcoms, the pair had previously worked together on many shows, including ''[[Parks and Recreation]]'', but had never written anything together before "Nosedive".<ref name="avclub interview"/> A fan of Brooker's works, Rashida Jones had been in contact with him for a few years beforehand and after the programme's move to Netflix, he suggested that she could write an episode. Schur was also a fan of ''Black Mirror'' and Rashida Jones suggested that they could co-write the episode. With Jones and Schur on board, the main character changed from someone focused on playing the ratings system to a people-pleaser, the work presentation was changed to a wedding and the idea of Lacie having a childhood talisman was introduced. Lacie's brother was originally an ex-boyfriend.<ref name="ibm"/>

Schur wrote the first half of the episode (up to Lacie beginning her travel in a rented car), while Rashida Jones wrote the second half, and the two then combined their scripts.<ref name="avclub interview"/> In the initial draft, the episode ended with Lacie's work presentation going viral and her achieving fame. The final version of the ending showed Lacie in a jail cell, the rating device removed from her, allowing her to find freedom. An unused idea was that of rage rooms, where characters would go to destroy things to let out their anger.<ref name="ibm"/>

In 2016, Schur had an account on [[Twitter]] but not [[Facebook]] or [[Instagram]], as "there's a bunch of strangers talking shit about you in there", and Jones expressed a similarly negative attitude, stating "I do have very strong, very conflicted feelings about rating systems and social media."<ref name="avclub interview">{{cite web|url=https://www.avclub.com/rashida-jones-and-michael-schur-talk-about-bringing-fun-1798254169|title=Rashida Jones and Michael Schur talk about bringing funny to ''Black Mirror''|work=[[The A.V. Club]]|last=Zuckerman|first=Esther|date=22 October 2016|access-date=1 September 2017|archive-date=25 November 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201125224911/https://tv.avclub.com/rashida-jones-and-michael-schur-talk-about-bringing-fun-1798254169|url-status=live}}</ref> Brooker notes that "you are rewarded for having a more extreme opinion" on social media; in the episode, as on the internet, almost all ratings given are either one or five stars.<ref name="slate interview">{{cite web|url=http://www.slate.com/blogs/browbeat/2016/10/21/the_stars_and_writers_of_black_mirror_on_the_disturbing_new_season.html|title=''Black Mirror''{{'}}s Stars and Writers on How They Made the Most Disturbing Season Yet|last=Adams|first=Sam|work=[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]]|date=21 October 2016|access-date=8 December 2017}}</ref> Similarly, Schur opines that social media causes people to exaggerate their behaviour, particularly their rudeness.<ref name="time"/>

Jones believes that the episode, as with all ''Black Mirror'' episodes, "pushes you into the near future", while Schur considers it to be more of a "parallel reality". Brooker has described the episode as "like a cross between ''[[Pleasantville (film)|Pleasantville]]'' and ''[[The Truman Show]]''".<ref name="ew interview">{{cite magazine|url=https://www.ew.com/article/2016/10/23/black-mirror-postmortem-interview-season-3|title=Black Mirror postmortem: Showrunner talks season 3 twists|date=21 October 2016|last=Hibberd|first=James|magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]]|access-date=24 October 2016}}</ref> Jones says the belief that "women are taught to be liked, and men are taught to be powerful", credited to [[Sheryl Sandberg]], is relevant to the episode, with Schur agreeing that Lacie's gender is important to the story,<ref name="slate interview"/> though Schur notes that edited images on social media are causing negative [[body image]] issues for men as well.<ref name="time">{{cite magazine|url=https://time.com/4538883/black-mirror-netflix-rashida-jones-mike-schur/|title=Rashida Jones and Mike Schur's ''Black Mirror'' Episode Will Make You Rethink How You Use Social Media|magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]]|last=Dockterman|first=Eliana|date=20 October 2016|access-date=27 December 2017}}</ref>

===Filming===
[[File:Joe Wright by Gage Skidmore.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Joe Wright]], the episode's director]]
The episode was the third in series three to be filmed.<ref name="ibm"/> [[Joe Wright]] directed the episode, [[Seamus McGarvey]] was [[director of photography]] and the production designers, working for [[VFX]] company Painting Practice, were Joel Collins<ref name="creative review"/> and James Foster.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://variety.com/2017/tv/awards/joe-wright-relished-polyester-fabric-black-mirror-after-period-films-1202460842/|title=Joe Wright Relished the Chance to Go Polyester in 'Black Mirror'|work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|last=Tobias|first=Scott|date=12 June 2017|access-date=3 May 2018}}</ref> The episode was shot in four weeks<ref name="variety"/> in [[Knysna]], [[South Africa]],<ref name="ibm"/> a coastal town five hours (by car) from [[Cape Town]] chosen as it felt like an American coastal town.<ref name="creative review"/><ref name="ibm"/> Series three episode "[[San Junipero]]" was also filmed in South Africa.<ref name="creative review">{{cite web|url=https://www.creativereview.co.uk/designing-black-mirror-interview-production-designer-joel-collins/|title=Black Mirror production designer Joel Collins on bringing Charlie Brooker's dystopian visions to life|work=[[Creative Review]]|last=Steven|first=Rachael|url-access=registration|date=16 November 2016|access-date=5 January 2018}}</ref>

In an interview with ''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]'', McGarvey noted that the episode was shot in [[4K resolution]] at the request of Netflix. He said the [[colour scheme]] was a mixture of [[wikt:duck-egg blue|duck-egg blue]], "peppermint green" and "strange [[peach (color)|peach colors]]", and that props and "even the drinks people are drinking" were chosen with care to create a "sickly pastel feel".<ref name="variety">{{cite web|url=https://variety.com/2017/tv/awards/emmys-black-mirror-seamus-mcgarvey-interview-1202520496/|title='Black Mirror' DP Seamus McGarvey Talks About Finding the 'Photographic Heart' of 'Nosedive'|work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|last=Turchiano|first=Danielle|date=16 August 2017|access-date=1 September 2017}}</ref> Wright said that he made almost no changes to the script's dialogue.<ref name="nofilmschool">{{cite podcast|url=https://nofilmschool.com/2017/07/black-mirror-joe-wright-and-owen-harris|title='Black Mirror': How Directors Joe Wright and Owen Harris Built Dystopian Worlds That Look Like Our Own [PODCAST]|website=No Film School|last=Fusco|first=Jon|date=24 October 2016|access-date=31 December 2017}}</ref> Brooker has said that Wright's pastel treatment was a "very strong visual idea that we had not foreseen".<ref name="independent podcast">{{cite podcast|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/tv/features/charlie-brooker-interview-black-mirror-season-4-twitter-episode-writer-westworld-screenwriting-a8090086.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220621/https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/tv/features/charlie-brooker-interview-black-mirror-season-4-twitter-episode-writer-westworld-screenwriting-a8090086.html |archive-date=21 June 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|title=Charlie Brooker interview: Black Mirror creator on season 4, plot option paralysis and being on Twitter less|website=[[The Independent]]|last=Hooton|first=Christopher|date=4 December 2017|access-date=31 December 2017}}</ref>

Brooker pointed out that directors of ''Black Mirror'' episodes (in this case, Wright) have more "power" than in serialised television shows, as "it is like making a short film", and he said that Wright had "been feeling quite bruised after doing ''[[Pan (2015 film)|Pan]]'', and [''Black Mirror''] was a good thing for him to get his teeth into which wasn't the full five-year commitment of a movie".<ref name="worst year ever"/> McGarvey had previously worked with Wright.<ref name="variety"/> Watching [[dailies|rushes]] from the filming, Brooker was initially sceptical about Wright's saccharine style, but began to understand it as the filming progressed and the music was added.<ref name="independent podcast"/> The scenes in which Lacie is driving utilise a [[computer-generated imagery|computer-generated]] landscape designed by Dan May, the episode's art director.<ref name="creative review"/> She was initially planned to drive through multiple landscapes such as a desert, but this was changed for budget reasons.<ref name="ibm"/>

Bryce Dallas Howard plays Lacie, the episode's main character. She was suggested by Wright, who auditioned her a decade previously for ''[[Atonement (2007 film)|Atonement]]''.<ref name="nofilmschool"/> Howard gained {{convert|30|lb|kg}} for the role, saying in an interview with ''[[Marie Claire]]'' that body shaming is a "huge part of the subtext of the story".<ref name="marie claire"/> She chose a laugh for Lacie which mixed "fear", "disingenuousness" and "depression".<ref name="ibm"/> Howard first joined social media during Thanksgiving 2015 and was approached with the [[film treatment|treatment]] of the episode a fortnight later, in December 2015.<ref name="marie claire">{{cite web|url=http://www.marieclaire.com/celebrity/news/a23270/bryce-dallas-howard-black-mirror-interview/|title=Bryce Dallas Howard on Body Image, Social Media, and Gaining 30 Pounds for 'Black Mirror'|last=Bonner|first=Mehera|work=[[Marie Claire]]|date=26 October 2016|access-date=3 September 2017}}</ref><ref name="cosmopolitan">{{cite web|url=http://www.cosmopolitan.com/entertainment/tv/a7666694/black-mirror-bryce-dallas-howard-alice-eve-nosedive-interview/|title=Black Mirror Stars on the Terrifying Episode That May Make You Delete Your Instagram|work=[[Cosmopolitan (magazine)|Cosmopolitan]]|last=Dibdin|first=Emma|date=28 October 2016|access-date=3 September 2017}}</ref>

===Music===
Chosen by Wright to compose the episode's soundtrack,<ref name="independent podcast"/> [[Max Richter]] is a self-described "conservatoire, university-trained classical composer".<ref name="Richter Atlantic">{{cite web|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/entertainment/archive/2016/11/max-richter-interview-black-mirror-the-leftovers-miss-sloane/506033/|title=Max Richter's Soundtrack to Dystopia|work=[[The Atlantic]]|last=Gilbert|first=Sophie|date=1 November 2016|access-date=12 August 2017}}</ref> Richter first met the director, Joe Wright, in London before the shooting of the episode had been completed and began coming up with ideas for the score. Richter aimed to "support" the episode's display of "incredible anxiety hovering beneath this smiley surface ... while at the same time not flattening out the emotionality of it", commenting in an interview that Wright's camerawork had a "dream-like quality" and that Brooker's "story was fantastic".<ref name="Richter Fact">{{cite web|url=http://www.factmag.com/2016/10/27/max-richter-soundtrack-black-mirror-nosedive/|title=Black Mirror composer Max Richter on soundtracking society's social media meltdown|work=[[Fact (UK magazine)|Fact]]|last=Warwick|first=Oli|date=27 October 2016|access-date=12 August 2017}}</ref>

In another interview, Richter said he was aiming for the episode to have "warmth and a fairytale quality throughout" with "darkness underneath it", and notes that his composition was based on "the sentiment and the emotional trajectory of the characters". Richter also composed the sound effects which play when one character rates another, and incorporated these sounds into the score itself.<ref name="Richter Atlantic"/>

==Analysis==
Adam Chitwood commented in ''Collider'' that Joe Wright deviated from his typical style, with visuals that focus on the characters.<ref name="collider">{{cite web|url=https://collider.com/black-mirror-season-3-review-san-junipero-nosedive/|title='Black Mirror' Season 3 Review: "San Junipero" and "Nosedive" Are a Sunny Start|last=Chitwood|first=Adam|publisher=[[Collider (website)|Collider]]|date=15 September 2016|access-date=19 September 2016}}</ref> The world is "extremely curated" and appears perfect, wrote ''[[Architectural Digest]]''{{'}}s Shelli Nicole, reflecting the theme of "popularity and validation from social media". Pastel colours—"soft and superficially sweet pinks, greens, and blues"—conceal the darkness in the world.<ref name="AD">{{cite web|url=https://www.architecturaldigest.com/story/black-mirror-has-always-excelled-at-dystopian-design|title=''Black Mirror'' Has Always Excelled at Dystopian Design—Here Are 5 Examples|work=[[Architectural Digest]]|last=Nicole|first=Shelli|date=16 June 2023|accessdate=2 January 2024|archive-date=19 July 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230719115516/https://www.architecturaldigest.com/story/black-mirror-has-always-excelled-at-dystopian-design|url-status=live}}</ref>

A ''[[Business Insider]]'' article by Erin Brodwin argued that Lacie falls victim to the [[hedonic treadmill]]. Despite momentary happiness when receiving a high rating, Lacie is "lonely and unsatisfied". Brodwin pointed out that scientific studies concur with Lacie's experience, because there is no correlation between using social media and being happy in the long-term.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.businessinsider.com/psychology-black-mirror-nosedive-social-media-2016-10|title=What psychology actually says about the tragically social-media obsessed society in 'Black Mirror'|work=[[Business Insider]]|last=Brodwin|first=Erin|date=27 October 2016|access-date=1 September 2017}}</ref>

===Comparisons to other media===
Several critics compared the episode to a 2014 episode of ''[[Community (TV series)|Community]]'', "[[App Development and Condiments]]", which features an app where users assign each other "Meow Meow Beenz" ratings on a scale from one to five; Jack Shepherd of ''[[The Independent]]'' noted that both episodes "critically [analyse] people's obsession with stature on social media platforms with rating systems".<ref name="Independent Community"/> Other reviewers compared "Nosedive" to the [[mobile application]] [[Peeple (mobile application)|Peeple]],<ref name="Atlantic">{{cite news|last1=Gilbert|first1=Sophie|title='Black Mirror' Is Back: 'Nosedive' Is a Sharp Satire About Social Media|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/entertainment/archive/2016/10/black-mirror-nosedive-review-season-three-netflix/504668/|access-date=22 October 2016|work=[[The Atlantic]]|date=21 October 2016}}</ref> in which users could rate one another, that garnered immediate backlash upon its release.<ref name="Atlantic"/><ref name="Decider"/> Brooker said in an interview that he was not aware of the ''Community'' episode when he came up with the idea for "Nosedive", but that he did see advertising for Peeple during pre-production, initially thinking it would turn out to be marketing for a comedy show, and he considered whether or not they should still produce the episode.<ref name="Decider">{{cite web|url=http://decider.com/2016/10/27/black-mirror-nosedive-did-not-steal-from-community-interview/|title=Did 'Black Mirror' Creator Charlie Brooker Know About That 'Community' Episode When He Made "Nosedive"?|last=Cobb|first=Kayla|work=Decider|publisher=[[New York Post]]|date=27 October 2016|access-date=12 August 2017}}</ref> The episode has also been compared to the 2003 novel ''[[Down and Out in the Magic Kingdom]]'', as each work explores a link between social approval and power.<ref name="verge"/>

Manuel Betancourt of ''[[Pacific Standard]]'' explained how "Nosedive" fits with other portrayals of social media in television and film, comparing it to 2017 films ''[[The Circle (2017 film)|The Circle]]'' and ''[[Ingrid Goes West]]'', which both explore negative aspects of social media. Betancourt said that historically, women have been portrayed as victims of technology, a pattern which these works fit. For instance, Ingrid and Lacie are both obsessed with coming across as perfect online. In contrast, male characters are traditionally the voice of reason: in these works, Lacie's brother Ryan, Mercer (''The Circle'') and Taylor's husband (''Ingrid Goes West'') serve this purpose.<ref name="pacific"/> The androgyny of "Nosedive" character Susan is linked to her disdain for social media.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://dailytitan.com/2017/04/female-gaze-black-mirror-explores-gendered-expectations-social-media/|title=The Female Gaze: 'Black Mirror' explores the gendered expectations of social media|work=[[The Daily Titan]]|last=Casas|first=Darlene|date=11 April 2017|access-date=27 December 2017}}</ref> Betancourt wrote that these characterisations do not accord with research on how men and women use technology, where some studies report that men have more emotional investment in positive feedback on social media. However, "Nosedive" shows people of all genders placing importance in social media, leading Betancourt to call it "perhaps the most keen-eyed critique [...] of recent titles".<ref name="pacific">{{cite news|url=https://psmag.com/social-justice/why-are-so-many-ladies-insta-fiends-in-movies|title=Why Does Hollywood Tell So Many Stories About Women Obsessed With Social Media?|work=[[Pacific Magazine]]|last=Betancourt|first=Manuel|date=11 August 2017|access-date=31 August 2017}}</ref>
An episode of ''The Orville'' released the same year features a similar idea, with the ship visiting a planet where people can rate each other, services and new products.

Critics also noted the inclusion of [[Easter egg (media)|Easter eggs]] within ''Black Mirror''&nbsp;– small details referring to other episodes. In "Nosedive", a social media post from Michael Callow reads, "Just got thrown out of the zoo again :(", a joke based on Callow having intercourse with a pig in "[[The National Anthem (Black Mirror)|The National Anthem]]".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.inverse.com/article/22898-black-mirror-season-3-easter-eggs|title=Every Single 'Black Mirror' Season 3 Easter Egg|work=[[Inverse (website)|Inverse]]|last=Hutchinson|first=Sean|date=28 October 2016|access-date=13 September 2017}}</ref> Brooker has described this Easter egg as his favourite in series three.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://decider.com/2016/11/03/netflix-black-mirror-charlie-brooker-annabel-jones-interview/|title='Black Mirror' Creators Talk About Season Three's Easter Eggs And What Your Favorite Episode Says About You|last=Cobb|first=Kayla|work=Decider|publisher=[[New York Post]]|date=3 November 2016|access-date=13 September 2017}}</ref> Another reference to that episode is the fictional show ''Sea of Tranquility''; in "The National Anthem", a special effects expert mentions having worked on the show, while in "Nosedive", Lacie hitchhikes with fans of the show. Additionally, in "[[Hated in the Nation]]", a news ticker contains the term "Reputelligent", which is the name of the company that Lacie consults for advice about her rating.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://screencrush.com/black-mirror-easter-eggs-theory/|title=24 Easter Eggs From All Three Seasons of 'Black Mirror', Plus a Timeline Connecting Every Episode|work=ScreenCrush|publisher=[[Townsquare Media]]|last=Whitney|first=Erin Oliver|date=26 October 2016 |access-date=13 September 2017}}</ref>

===Comparisons to credit ratings===
"Nosedive" was widely compared to China's [[Social Credit System]], a government initiative which began pilot projects in 2014,<ref name="Wired"/> initially using private systems such as [[Sesame Credit]].<ref name="dog SCS">{{cite web|url=https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/how-black-mirror-season-3-is-eerily-coming-true/|title=How Black Mirror series 3 is eerily coming true|work=[[Den of Geek!]]|publisher=[[Dennis Publishing]]|last=Leane|first=Rob|date=3 November 2016|access-date=12 August 2017}}</ref><ref name="BM&Philosophy">{{Citation|last1=Urueña|first1=Sergio|chapter=Nosedive and the Anxieties of Social Media|date=2019|title=Black Mirror and Philosophy|pages=81–91|publisher=John Wiley & Sons, Ltd|language=en|doi=10.1002/9781119578291.ch8|isbn=978-1-119-57829-1|last2=Melikyan|first2=Nonna|s2cid=213954986}}</ref> The state projects were implemented differently by local governments, but each collected data on citizens in order to assign them an overall score.<ref name="Wired">{{cite magazine|url=https://www.wired.co.uk/article/china-social-credit-system-explained|title=The complicated truth about China's social credit system|magazine=[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]]|last=Kobie|first=Nicole|date=7 June 2019|access-date=6 May 2021}}</ref> An example plan saw the scores determine whether a citizen would be allowed to take out a loan or what quality of school their child would go to. Actions such as defaulting on a loan or being critical of the government would decrease a person's score. By the time "Nosedive" was released, the Sesame Credit system, which assigned users scores between 350 and 950,<ref name="tele SCS"/> allowed some people with high scores to rent vehicles without a deposit, or pay to skip hospital queues.<ref name="dog SCS"/><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/asia_pacific/chinas-plan-to-organize-its-whole-society-around-big-data-a-rating-for-everyone/2016/10/20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190211022649/https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/asia_pacific/chinas-plan-to-organize-its-whole-society-around-big-data-a-rating-for-everyone/2016/10/20/|url-status=dead|archive-date=11 February 2019|title=China's plan to organize its society relies on 'big data' to rate everyone|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|last=Denyer|first=Simon|date=22 October 2016|access-date=19 March 2018}}</ref> Furthermore, a person's score in Sesame Credit was dependent on the scores of the people in their social circle.<ref name="tele SCS">{{cite news | url = https://www.telegraph.co.uk/on-demand/2017/12/15/black-mirror-coming-true-china-rating-affects-home-transport/| title =Black Mirror is coming true in China, where your 'rating' affects your home, transport and social circle | first = Alice | last = Vincent | date = 15 December 2017 | access-date = 19 March 2018 | work =[[The Daily Telegraph]] }}</ref>

The proposed and existing systems were widely compared to the episode as a whole. For example, the apartment discount Lacie hopes for is similar to how high-rated people under Sesame Credit could rent cars without a deposit.<ref name="avclub SCS">{{cite web | url = https://www.avclub.com/at-least-one-black-mirror-episode-is-already-coming-tru-1821315524 | title = At least one Black Mirror episode is already coming true in China | first = William | last = Hughes | date = 15 December 2017 | access-date = 15 December 2017 | work = [[The A.V. Club]] }}</ref> Additionally, Lacie's ejection from the airport is reminiscent of the system's control over who can partake in some forms of transport.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.esquire.com/news-politics/a19467976/black-mirror-social-credit-china/|title=A 'Black Mirror' Episode Is Coming to Life in China|work=[[Esquire (magazine)|Esquire]]|last=Bruney|first=Gabrielle|date=17 March 2018|access-date=19 March 2018}}</ref>

Brooker has commented on "Nosedive" and the Social Credit System. He joked in an interview, "I promise you we didn't sell the idea to the Chinese government!" About seeing the concept of the episode come to life in the real world, Brooker said: "It was quite trippy".<ref>{{cite news | url =  https://www.thedailybeast.com/black-mirror-creator-charlie-brooker-on-chinas-social-credit-system-and-the-rise-of-trump | title = 'Black Mirror' Creator Charlie Brooker on China's 'Social Credit' System and the Rise of Trump | first = Marlow | last = Stern | date = 27 October 2016 | access-date = 15 December 2017 | work = [[The Daily Beast]] }}</ref> He commented that a key difference between China's plans and the one in "Nosedive" is "that there's a central government assessing things. Being state-controlled, it feels even more sinister". He said the Social Credit System "sounds like an attempt to make the population behave in a particular way".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.shortlist.com/entertainment/tv/black-mirror-charlie-brooker-interview/334899|title=We got Charlie Brooker to rate real life 'Black Mirror' events|last=Sayer|first=Chris|work=[[ShortList]]|date=22 November 2017|access-date=25 December 2017}}</ref> In November 2016, the Facebook page for ''Black Mirror'' shared an article in ''[[The Washington Post]]'' about the Social Credit System.{{efn|group=note|The article shared was the following: {{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/asia_pacific/chinas-plan-to-organize-its-whole-society-around-big-data-a-rating-for-everyone/2016/10/20/1cd0dd9c-9516-11e6-ae9d-0030ac1899cd_story.html|title=China's plan to organize its society relies on 'big data' to rate everyone|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|last=Denyer|first=Simon|date=22 October 2016}}}}

Julien Migozzi found similarities between the episode and the segregation that South Africans face under [[credit score]] systems.<ref name="Migozzi">{{cite journal |last1=Migozzi |first1=Julien |title=Apartheid by Algorithm |journal=Logic Magazine |date=August 22, 2022 |issue=17 |url=https://logicmag.io/home/apartheid-by-algorithm/ |access-date=26 September 2022 |language=en}}</ref>

==Reception==
[[Adam Mosseri]], the CEO of social network [[Instagram]], said he was inspired by "Nosedive" to test the hiding of "likes" on the Instagram service starting in 2019, recognising the negative connotations that keeping the number of "likes" easily visible had on some users' behaviour.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.nytimes.com/2020/01/17/business/instagram-likes.html | title = This Is the Guy Who's Taking Away the Likes | first = Amy | last = Chozick | date = 17 January 2020 | access-date = 20 January 2020 | work = [[The New York Times]] }}</ref>

The episode was parodied in the 2017 ''[[Saturday Night Live]]'' sketch "Five Stars". It features [[Aziz Ansari]] and [[Bobby Moynihan]] desperately trying to impress each other on an [[Uber]] ride to boost each other's ratings. The sketch explicitly mentions ''Black Mirror'', with both characters saying that "San Junipero" is their favourite episode.<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://ew.com/recap/saturday-night-live-season-42-episode-12/|title=''Saturday Night Live'' recap: Aziz Ansari|magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]]|last=Holub|first=Christian|date=22 January 2017|access-date=13 September 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.avclub.com/aziz-ansari-confidently-anchors-a-uniformly-strong-satu-1798190103|title=Aziz Ansari confidently anchors a uniformly strong ''Saturday Night Live''|work=[[The A.V. Club]]|last=Perkins|first=Dennis|date=22 January 2017|access-date=13 September 2017}}</ref>

That same year, the episode was parodied in [[The Amazing World of Gumball]] episode "The Stars" in which [[Richard Watterson]] gives Larry's hairdressing job a bad review, leading to Larry giving him his haircut for free. This influences [[Gumball (fictional cat)|Gumball]] and [[Darwin (fictional fish)|Darwin]] go reviewing the places Larry works to get various amenities for free, which leads to chaos.

===Critical reception===
{{quote box|align=right|bgcolor=lavender|width=28%|quote=Behind her pink and perky [[façade]], Lacie becomes obsessed with social media status in "Nosedive", an episode that demonstrates the dangers of society's need for approval but does so with a perfect dose of humor.|source=–Critics' consensus on [[Rotten Tomatoes]]<ref name="RottenTomatoes"/>}}
"Nosedive" was well received by critics. Review aggregator website [[Rotten Tomatoes]] collected 22 reviews, identified 95% of them as positive, and calculated an average rating of 7.33/10.<ref name="RottenTomatoes">{{cite web|url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/tv/black_mirror/s03/e01|title=Black Mirror – Season 3, Episode 1 – Rotten Tomatoes|publisher=[[Rotten Tomatoes]]|access-date=24 July 2020}}</ref> The episode garnered four-star ratings in ''The Independent'' and ''[[The Guardian]]'',<ref name="independent">{{cite web|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/tv/reviews/black-mirror-season-3-episode-3-s03e03-review-release-date-spoilers-charlie-brooker-netflix-bryce-a7342551.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220621/https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/tv/reviews/black-mirror-season-3-episode-3-s03e03-review-release-date-spoilers-charlie-brooker-netflix-bryce-a7342551.html |archive-date=21 June 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|title=Black Mirror season 3 episode 1 review: 'A temporary puppeteer of your thoughts'|work=[[The Independent]]|last=Stolworthy|first=Jacob|date=3 October 2016|access-date=3 September 2017}}</ref><ref name="Guardian Lee">{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2016/sep/16/black-mirror-first-look-review-charlie-brooker|title=Black Mirror review – Charlie Brooker's splashy new series is still a sinister marvel|work=[[The Guardian]]|date=16 September 2016|access-date=19 September 2016|last=Lee|first=Benjamin}}</ref> along with an A− rating in ''[[The A.V. Club]]''.<ref name="avclub">{{cite web|url=https://www.avclub.com/black-mirror-returns-please-swipe-right-1798189216|title=''Black Mirror'' returns, please swipe right|work=[[The A.V. Club]]|last=Handlen|first=Zack|date=21 October 2016|access-date=12 August 2017}}</ref> In ''[[The Mancunion]]'', the episode received 3.5 stars;<ref name="mancunion">{{cite web|url=http://mancunion.com/2016/11/15/review-black-mirror-s3e01-nosedive/|title=Review: Black Mirror S3E01 — Nosedive|work=[[The Mancunion]]|last=Setranah|first=Emefa|date=15 November 2016|access-date=3 September 2017}}</ref> it was rated three stars by ''[[The Daily Telegraph|The Telegraph]]'' and the ''[[Irish Independent]]''.<ref name="telegraph">{{cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/on-demand/0/black-mirror-season-3-nosedive-review-a-thought-provoking-pastel/|title=Black Mirror, season 3, Nosedive, review: 'a thought-provoking, pastel-coloured hell'|work=[[The Daily Telegraph|The Telegraph]]|last=Monahan|first=Mark|date=21 October 2016|access-date=12 August 2017}}</ref><ref name="irish">{{cite web|url=http://www.independent.ie/entertainment/television/tv-reviews/black-mirror-is-back-and-its-as-disturbing-as-ever-with-a-few-minor-cracks-35156063.html|title=Black Mirror is back and it's as disturbing as ever... with a few minor cracks|work=[[Irish Independent]]|last=Stacey|first=Pat|date=24 October 2016|access-date=3 September 2017}}</ref> Emefa Setranah of ''The Mancunion'' wrote that the episode lives up to the show's reputation,<ref name="mancunion"/> and ''The Guardian''{{'s}} Benjamin Lee said the episode feels fresh despite covering technology similarly to prior episodes.<ref name="Guardian Lee"/>

Charles Bramesco wrote in ''[[Vulture (magazine)|Vulture]]'' that it expresses the show's "guiding theme" with "lucid clarity".<ref name="vulture ranking"/> ''[[TheWrap]]'' authors praised how the episode tackles society's social media obsession,<ref name="wrap ranking"/> and Mat Elfring of [[GameSpot]] said that its thought-provoking nature makes it a good choice for the season premiere.<ref name="gamespot ranking"/> Matt Fowler wrote for [[IGN]] that the episode is "both fun and frustrating" which contrasts with the "grounded and grim" episodes to follow.<ref name="ign">{{cite web|url=https://ign.com/articles/2016/10/19/black-mirror-season-3-review|title=BLACK MIRROR: SEASON 3 REVIEW|publisher=[[IGN]]|first=Matt|last=Fowler|date=October 19, 2016|access-date=October 20, 2016}}</ref> ''[[Esquire (magazine)|Esquire]]''{{'s}} Corey Atad opined that it is "a tad too simplistic" though "totally engaging".<ref name="esquire ranking"/> Pat Stacey criticised in the ''Irish Independent'' that it "sets up the premise crisply, then spends far too much time labouring the point."<ref name="irish"/>

A major criticism was the episode's predictability and repetitiveness,<ref name="mancunion"/><ref name="comingsoon"/> while reception to the ending was mixed. Aubrey Page on ''[[Collider (website)|Collider]]'' called the episode "woefully surface-level and a bit off-brand" because of its predictability,<ref name="collider ranking"/> with ''Variety''{{'s}} Andrew Wallenstein agreeing and further saying that the episode lacks a disturbing tone, though this makes it more accessible.<ref name="variety ranking"/> Zack Handlen of ''The A.V. Club'' believed that the first half of "Nosedive" is too predictable but the second half "[adds] depth and sincerity".<ref name="avclub"/> Tasha Robinson wrote for ''[[The Verge]]'' that the episode "can be strident and obvious" but "understands human nature very well".<ref name="verge"/> Some reviewers believed the episode was too long and the ending was too positive.<ref name="Atlantic"/><ref name="avclub"/> However, ''[[Digital Spy]]''{{'s}} Alex Mullane praised the ending, because though it is "bleak in some ways" it is also "a moment of sheer, fist-pumping joy";<ref name="ds"/> Jacob Hall agreed in ''[[/Film]]'', calling the ending "simultaneously cathartic and on-the-nose".<ref name="slash ranking"/>

Critics had a mostly positive response to the script as a whole, with some noting comedic undertones.<ref name="ew ranking"/> Robinson described the episode as an "exaggerated morality play about the dangers of conformity and the small pleasures of individuality".<ref name="verge">{{cite web|url=https://www.theverge.com/2016/10/24/13379204/black-mirror-season-3-episode-1-nosedive-recap|title=Black Mirror's third season opens with a vicious take on social media|work=[[The Verge]]|last=Robinson|first=Tasha|date=24 October 2016|access-date=12 August 2017}}</ref> The script has been called "bitingly hilarious",<ref name="collider"/> "funny", "uplifting",<ref name="ds">{{cite web|url=http://www.digitalspy.com/tv/black-mirror/review/a811645/black-mirror-season-3-review-the-surprise-climax-to-nosedive-is-the-shows-biggest-twist-yet/|title=Black Mirror season 3 'Nosedive' review: this one contains the show's biggest twist yet|work=[[Digital Spy]]|last=Mullane|first=Alex|date=22 October 2016|access-date=3 September 2017}}</ref> "moving" and "supremely unsettling".<ref name="vulture ranking"/> Lee approved of the script avoiding [[exposition (narrative)|exposition]].<ref name="Guardian Lee"/> On the other hand, ''The Telegraph''{{'s}} Mark Monahan criticised that the plot and characters do not live up to their potential.<ref name="telegraph"/> Page felt the episode "lacks the sadistic snap of Brooker's usual work".<ref name="collider ranking"/>

[[File:Max Richter - 2015 - ATP Festival.png|thumb|alt=Max Richter performing as a pianist|[[Max Richter]]'s soundtrack for the episode was praised by reviewers.]]

The episode's visual style and Joe Wright's directing were highly commended;<ref name="independent"/> the setting for the episode garnered positive reception.<ref name="collider"/><ref name="Guardian Lee"/><ref name="telegraph"/> ''Architectural Digest'' reviewed it as the best design of the third series.<ref name="AD"/> Hall complimented "stellar production values".<ref name="slash ranking"/> [[Sophie Gilbert]] of ''[[The Atlantic]]'' praises the juxtaposition of calm visuals with narrative tension.<ref name="Atlantic"/> Robinson noted that the aesthetics mark a difference between the characters with high and low ratings.<ref name="verge"/> Setranah noted that Netflix's large budget is apparent in the visuals of the episode,<ref name="mancunion"/> and ''The Independent'' writers suggested it is detailed enough to be revisited.<ref name="independent ranking"/>

Many critics praised Howard's performance,<ref name="avclub"/><ref name="mancunion"/> with Atad calling it "delightfully unhinged".<ref name="esquire ranking"/> Additionally, Gilbert wrote that Howard "conveys Lacie's inner frustration while grinning cheerfully through it".<ref name="Atlantic"/> Howard's acting ensures viewers are on Lacie's side, according to Mullane, who also compliments Eve's acting as "excellent".<ref name="ds"/>

Max Richter's musical composition for the episode was well-received. ''The Independent'' writers complimented Richter for "blending the [[diegetic music|diegetic]] sounds of the app with the non-diegetic score evoking our protagonist's struggle to determine reality and fiction",<ref name="independent"/> an element which Robinson also praised.<ref name="verge"/> Fowler called the score "very compelling"<ref name="ign"/> and Monahan described it as "elegantly elegiac".<ref name="telegraph"/>

==Board game==
Based on the episode, the board game ''Nosedive'' was produced by [[Asmodee]]. Released on 25 November 2018, the game requires between three and six players and is designed to last for roughly 45 minutes.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.polygon.com/2018/11/15/18097545/black-mirror-nosedive-board-game-asmodee | title = Black Mirror's nightmarish social media episode is now a board game | first = Michael | last = McWhertor | date = 15 November 2018 | access-date = 1 July 2019 | work = [[Polygon (website)|Polygon]] }}</ref> A mobile app, available for [[Android (operating system)|Android]] or [[iOS]], is used to play the game; it initially assigns each player a Social Score. In the initial Lifestyle phase, players draw cards which have ratings between one and five stars, such as the one star card "A six-minute lunch break". They tactically assign them to stacks and then each player selects a stack.<ref name="Verge board game"/>

In the Experience phase, players assign each other experiences such as "Receiving an anonymous hate cake" and each player then rates their received experiences from one to five stars. The app then adjusts each player's Social Score based on these ratings. At the end of the game, players earn points from the Lifestyle cards they own which have star ratings less than or equal to their Social Score.<ref name="Verge board game">{{cite web|url=https://www.theverge.com/2018/12/8/18120393/black-mirror-nosedive-card-app-game-asmodee-review|title=The Black Mirror card game isn't soul-crushing enough to reflect the show|work=[[The Verge]]|last=Robinson|first=Tasha|date=8 December 2018|access-date=1 July 2019}}</ref>

Tasha Robinson of ''[[The Verge]]'' criticised the game's mechanics as feeling arbitrary, as users' Social Scores are mostly determined by random factors. However, Robinson praised the app's design, the game's pastel aesthetics and the humour of the Experience cards, which can lead to interesting discussion.<ref name="Verge board game"/>
